[[Carrère and Hastings]] | architecture = Late Victorian, French Renaissance | added = January 12, 1981 | area = {{convert|359.7|acre}} | ref_num = 81000392{{NRISref|version=2010a|refnum=81000392}} }} '''Branch Brook Park''' is a [[Essex County Park System|county park]] of [[Essex County, New Jersey]]. It is located in the North Ward of [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]], between the neighborhoods of [[Forest Hill, Newark, New Jersey|Forest Hill]] and [[Roseville, Newark, New Jersey|Roseville]]. A portion of the park is also located within the Township of Belleville. At {{convert|360|acre}}, Branch Brook Park is the largest public park in the city of [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]]. The park is noted for the largest collection of [[cherry blossom]] trees in the United States, having over 5,000 in more than eighteen different varieties collectively called '''Cherryblossomland''', as well as a Cherry Blossom Festival each April.{{cite web |title=Student scientists track nation's largest collection of cherry blossom trees at Essex County park |publisher=The Star-Ledger |date=August 13, 2010 |url=https://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2010/08/aspiring_scientists_track_coun.html |access-date=2012-04-10}}{{cite web |last=Hinds |first=Kate |title=Cherry Blossom Trees Flourish in Newark |publisher=WNYC |date=March 25, 2012 |url=http://culture.wnyc.org/articles/features/2012/mar/25/newarks-cherry-blossom-trees |access-date=2012-04-10 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120331004048/http://culture.wnyc.org/articles/features/2012/mar/25/newarks-cherry-blossom-trees/ |archive-date=2012-03-31 }}{{cite news|last1=Di Ionno|first1=Mark|title=The story behind Branch Brook Park's cherry blossom trees|url=https://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2016/03/the_story_behind_branch_brook_parks_cherry_blossom.html|access-date=9 February 2018|work=The Star-Ledger|date=27 March 2016}} The park is home to many architecturally significant structures, including bridges, buildings, gates, and sculptures. Many of these were designed by the beaux-arts architectural firm of [[Carrère and Hastings]] headed by John Merven Carrère and [[Thomas Hastings (architect)|Thomas Hastings]]. The pair designed two Subway Bridges now referred to as Subway 1, East and Subway 2, West.{{cite web |title=Branch Brook Park Subway Bridges |url=https://www.bridgesnyc.com/2014/12/branch-brook-park-subway-bridges/ |website=bridgesnyc.com |date=December 23, 2014 |access-date=2015-01-22}} == History == The area had served as an [[Union Army|Army]] training ground during the [[American Civil War]]. At the time, the northern portion of the area had been a marsh known as Old Blue Jay Swamp. In 1867, [[Frederick Law Olmsted]] and [[Calvert Vaux]], the designers of [[Central Park]], presented their report on the site to the Board of Commissioners of the Newark Park.{{cite web |last1=Olmsted |first1=Frederick Law |last2=Vaux |first2=Calvert | author-link1=Frederick Law Olmsted | author-link2 = Calvert Vaux |title=Report on a site for a Park at Newark |url=https://dana.njit.edu/files/original/013ae6b1dd6f25b8ea37881bae023571.pdf |website=Digital Archive of Newark Architecture |publisher=[[New Jersey Institute of Technology]] |access-date=25 April 2023}} It recommended Concourse Hill, with its commanding views of Newark and distant Manhattan, as the best location for the park.{{cite web |title=Reviving Newark's Branch Brook Park |url=https://dana.njit.edu/files/original/5b1e6a1247eceb790a6c24d437bbcc45.pdf |website=Digital Archive of Newark Architecture |publisher=[[New Jersey Institute of Technology]] |access-date=25 April 2023}} Originally published by [https://www.preservationnj.org/ Preservation New Jersey] in ''Preservation Perspective''. However, the [[New Jersey State Legislature]] did not approve the $1 million required to acquire and improve the land. By the time the plan was re-visited 28 years later, only a third of the original {{convert|700|acre}} that was envisioned was available for twice the cost.Stuart Galishoff, ''Newark: the nation's unhealthiest city, 1832-1895'' (1988).{{cite web|url=https://www.thefreelibrary.com/Newark%3A+The+Nation's+Unhealthiest+City,+1832-1895.-a0150872451|title=Newark: The Nation's Unhealthiest City, 1832-1895.|website=thefreelibrary.com|access-date=February 10, 2025}} The park was formally created almost three decades later, in 1895, by the newly created [[Essex County Park System, New Jersey|Essex County Parks Commission]], making it the nation's first county park. In 1898, a public appropriation financed the conversion of the swamp into a landscaped lake. The initial park was only {{convert|60|acre}} in size but grew in the 1920s through private donations from prominent Newark families, such as the Ballantines, eventually reaching the city limit with [[Belleville, New Jersey|Belleville]] and becoming one of the largest urban parks in the United States. The [[Morris Canal]] originally ran on the park's west side, until its old bed was turned into the [[Newark Light Rail|Newark City Subway]], providing access to the park from [[Downtown Newark]]. The first designs of the park, based largely on romantic garden themes, were proposed in 1895 and 1898, after the Parks Commission hired several architectural firms to plan the park. In 1900, the commission hired the [[Olmsted Brothers]] firm to redesign the park. The result was the park's current naturalistic look and feel, with acres of meadows and forests, in a manner similar to [[Frederick Law Olmsted|their father's]] earlier designs of [[Central Park]] and [[Prospect Park, Brooklyn, New York|Prospect Park]]. [[File:Branchbrook Park.jpg|thumb|Cherry blossoms in Branch Brook Park]] The famous cherry trees were the result of a 1927 gift from [[Caroline Bamberger Fuld]], sister of department store magnate [[Louis Bamberger]] and widow of the store's vice president. The Cherry Blossom Festival attracts approximately 10,000 visitors each April. Branch Brook Park also features a lake and a pond. During [[World War II]], the park's grounds served a [[tent city]] for recruits, as well as a landing strip for airplanes of the [[United States Postal Service]]. The neighborhood on the east side of the park, [[Forest Hill, Newark, New Jersey|Forest Hill]], is Newark's most affluent. Also on the east side of the park is the [[Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart, Newark, New Jersey|Cathedral of the Sacred Heart Basilica]], one of the largest cathedrals in the United States. It has been placed on both the [[New Jersey Register of Historic Places|New Jersey]] (1980) and [[National Register of Historic Places|National]] (1981) Registers of Historic Places. === Roller rink === In 1956, a former reservoir was converted to a skating rink to accommodate requests for year-round ice-skating facilities. In October 1957, it opened to the public, featuring dancing and roller-skating in the summer. Before December of that year, 50,000 skaters used the facility for ice-hockey and figure skating.[https://web.archive.org/web/20240620174447/https://branchbrookpark.org/uploads/1/3/1/7/131747681/bbp_clr_vol2_-_history_of_the_park.pdf History of the Park and Critical Periods of Development], 2002 In 1961, funds from a [[New Jersey Department of Transportation]] park sale purchase were used to fund an enlarged entrance and 230-car parking area. The structure was enclosed in 1969 for all-weather use. The present roller rink was designed circa 1992.{{Clarification needed|reason="Designed" how? Wasn't it already built? This is what the source says.|date=December 2024}} Its current iteration, [[Branch Brook Park Roller Skating Center]], opened in 1996, is managed by national roller rink chain [[United Skates of America]]. The 12,000-foot roller rink building is located within the park, and has a contract with Essex County for Branch Brook.{{Cite web |last=NJ.com |first=Nyah Marshall {{!}} NJ Advance Media for |date=2024-03-16 |title=Inside N.J.'s booming Black roller skating scene |url=https://www.nj.com/news/2024/03/inside-njs-booming-black-roller-skating-scene.html |access-date=2024-12-18 |website=nj |language=en}} In 2013, ''[[NJ.com]]'' described the rink as "a symbol of revitalization for Newark" and "a literal savior of urban skating", exemplifying its relationship to the community, including [[roller derby]], [[Artistic roller skating|style skating]], gospel skaters, and DJ nightlife.{{Cite web |last=NJ.com |first=Amy Kuperinsky {{!}} NJ Advance Media for |date=2013-05-30 |title=Wheels keep on turning: 'The Rink' documents Newark's last roller skating haven |url=https://www.nj.com/entertainment/2013/05/rink_branch_brook_newark_film.html |access-date=2024-12-18 |website=nj |language=en}} === Restoration === In 1999, Branch Brook Park began a $25 million ten-year restoration program. In 2004, the Park Avenue bridge was repaired, as were the baseball fields in the center of the park. In 2007, a plan was created to provide for more than 5,000 cherry trees in the park and renovate and rename the Welcome Center. The plan uses a $650,000 grant from the Essex County Recreation and the Open Space Trust Fund from 2006 and private donations.[http://www.essex-countynj.org/index.php?section=essex/2007 The County of Essex, New Jersey]. Press Release. July 30, 2007. Retrieved May 29, 2012 In 2012, statues dedicated to sports figures [[Althea Gibson]] and [[Roberto Clemente]] were unveiled in the park.{{citation |last=Lee |first=Eunice |title=Statue of first black woman to win Wimbledon unveiled in Newark park |newspaper=The Star-Ledger |date=March 29, 2012 |url=https://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2012/03/statue_of_first_black_woman_to.html |access-date=2012-06-30 }}{{citation |last1=Simpri |first1=Arlene |last2=Strunsky |first2=Sterve |title=Roberto Clemente bronze statue unveiled in Newark's Branch Brook Park |newspaper=The Star-Ledger |date=June 3, 2012 |url=https://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2012/06/roberto_clemente_bronze_statue.html |access-date=2012-06-04 }} In 2013 the park was in the final phase of the restoration plan.{{Cite web |title=Essex County Branch Brook Park: Newark, New Jersey |url=https://www.planning.org/greatplaces/spaces/2013/branchbrookpark.htm |access-date=2022-04-22 |website=American Planning Association}} ==Gallery== Branch Brook Park.JPG|Branch Brook Park in [[Newark, New Jersey]] during the Cherry Blossom Festival Ballantine Gates @ Branch Brook Park.JPG|The Ballantine gates, on the east side of the park by [[Forest Hill, Newark, New Jersey|Forest Hill]], were given to Branch Brook Park by [[Peter Ballantine]] in 1899. They are modeled on gates in Scotland.
